P.title: P.blurb
Philosophy: Big questions, ethics, the mind, ways to live and good arguments.

P.title: ph-greeks.q0.q
Philosophy: What did Socrates claim to know?

P.title: ph-greeks.q0.x
Philosophy: Knowing your limits is the start of wisdom.

P.title: ph-greeks.q1.q
Philosophy: In Plato's cave, what do the prisoners see?

P.title: ph-greeks.c0.text
Philosophy: Philosophy means "love of wisdom". It asks questions science can't settle by experiment alone: what is real, what can we know, how should we live?

P.title: ph-greeks.c1.text
Philosophy: The first Greek philosophers looked for natural explanations instead of myths. Thales said everything was water; Heraclitus said everything flows; Democritus imagined atoms.

P.title: ph-greeks.c2.text
Philosophy: Socrates (c. 470–399 BCE) wrote nothing. He questioned people in the streets of Athens until they saw the gaps in what they thought they knew. Athens sentenced him to death.

P.title: ph-greeks.c3.title
Philosophy: I know that I know nothing

P.title: ph-greeks.c3.text
Philosophy: Socrates' wisdom was knowing the limits of his knowledge. "The unexamined life is not worth living" is his best-known line, from Plato's *Apology*.

P.title: ph-greeks.c3.viz.items.0.r
Philosophy: What would show me I'm wrong?

P.title: ph-greeks.c4.text
Philosophy: Plato imagined prisoners chained in a cave who see only shadows on the wall and take them for reality. Philosophy is the painful climb out into the sunlight.

P.title: ph-greeks.c5.text
Philosophy: Plato believed that behind changing things are perfect, eternal Forms: many circles exist, but each is an imperfect copy of the perfect Circle we understand with reason.

P.title: ph-greeks.c6.text
Philosophy: Plato's student Aristotle (384–322 BCE) studied almost everything: logic, biology, physics, politics, poetry. He tutored Alexander the Great and founded the Lyceum.

P.title: ph-greeks.c7.text
Philosophy: For Aristotle, virtue sits between two extremes. Courage lies between cowardice and recklessness; generosity between stinginess and wastefulness.

P.title: ph-greeks.c8.text
Philosophy: Aristotle's aim of life was eudaimonia, often translated as flourishing: living well by using reason and practising virtue, not just feeling good.

P.title: ph-greeks.c9.text
Philosophy: Teachers, lawyers and coaches still use Socratic questioning: instead of giving answers, they ask questions that help you examine your own reasoning.

P.title: ph-greeks.c9.viz.items.0
Philosophy: What do you mean by that?

P.title: ph-ethics.summary
Philosophy: How should we decide what's right?

P.title: ph-ethics.q0.q
Philosophy: Which theory judges actions by their consequences?

P.title: ph-ethics.q0.x
Philosophy: The greatest happiness for the greatest number.

P.title: ph-ethics.q1.o1
Philosophy: Designing society without knowing your place in it

P.title: ph-ethics.c0.text
Philosophy: Most ethical theories focus on one of three things: the consequences of an action, the duties or rules involved, or the character of the person acting.

P.title: ph-ethics.c1.text
Philosophy: Jeremy Bentham and John Stuart Mill argued that the right action produces the greatest happiness for the greatest number of people.

P.title: ph-ethics.c2.text
Philosophy: Immanuel Kant argued some things are wrong whatever the consequences. His test: act only on a rule you could want everyone to follow.

P.title: ph-ethics.c2.viz.items.0.r
Philosophy: Could everyone lie whenever it helps? Then trust collapses

P.title: ph-ethics.c3.text
Philosophy: Kant also said: never treat people merely as a means to your goals, but always also as ends in themselves, with their own dignity.

P.title: ph-ethics.c4.text
Philosophy: Rather than asking "what rule applies?", virtue ethics asks "what would a good person do?" and focuses on building traits like honesty, courage and kindness.

P.title: ph-ethics.c5.text
Philosophy: A runaway trolley will kill five people. You can pull a lever to divert it, killing one instead. Most people would pull. But would you push someone off a bridge to stop it? Most say no.

P.title: ph-ethics.c6.text
Philosophy: Two drivers text at the wheel; one hits a child, the other gets home safely. Their choices were equally bad, but we judge them very differently.

P.title: ph-ethics.c7.text
Philosophy: John Rawls asked: what society would you design if you didn't know who you'd be in it, rich or poor, healthy or ill? He thought you'd protect the worst off.

P.title: ph-ethics.c8.text
Philosophy: David Hume noticed that you can't get an "ought" from an "is" alone. "Smoking harms health" doesn't by itself mean "you shouldn't smoke"; you need a value too.

P.title: ph-ethics.c9.text
Philosophy: A doctor has five patients needing organs and one healthy visitor. A utilitarian sum seems to say sacrifice one; nearly everyone says no. Testing theories against cases is how ethics progresses.

P.title: ph-mind.summary
Philosophy: What can we know? What is a mind?

P.title: ph-mind.q1.q
Philosophy: According to Popper, a scientific theory must be…

P.title: ph-mind.c0.text
Philosophy: René Descartes tried to doubt everything: senses can deceive, dreams feel real. The one thing he couldn't doubt was that he was doubting: "I think, therefore I am."

P.title: ph-mind.c1.text
Philosophy: Rationalists like Descartes said knowledge comes mainly from reason. Empiricists like Locke and Hume said it comes from experience; the mind starts as a blank slate.

P.title: ph-mind.c2.text
Philosophy: The Sun has risen every day, so we expect it tomorrow. Hume pointed out we can't prove that the future will be like the past; we just assume it.

P.title: ph-mind.c3.text
Philosophy: Karl Popper argued a scientific theory must be testable in a way that could prove it wrong. "All swans are white" is scientific: one black swan refutes it.

P.title: ph-mind.c3.viz.items.0.r
Philosophy: What result would prove it wrong?

P.title: ph-mind.c4.text
Philosophy: How does the physical brain produce thoughts and feelings? Dualists say mind and body are different things; physicalists say the mind is what the brain does.

P.title: ph-mind.c5.text
Philosophy: Philosopher David Chalmers asked why brain activity feels like anything at all. Explaining what the brain does is "easy"; explaining why there's an inner experience is "hard".

P.title: ph-mind.c6.title
Philosophy: What is it like to be a bat?

P.title: ph-mind.c6.text
Philosophy: Thomas Nagel argued that even knowing everything about a bat's echolocation wouldn't tell us what it's like to experience it from the inside.

P.title: ph-mind.c6.viz.steps.0
Philosophy: Know every fact about bat brains

P.title: ph-mind.c7.text
Philosophy: John Searle imagined a person following a rulebook to answer Chinese questions perfectly without understanding Chinese. Does a computer understand, or just manipulate symbols?

P.title: ph-mind.c8.text
Philosophy: If every plank of a ship is replaced over time, is it the same ship? Your cells renew too. What makes you the same person over your life: memory, body, or something else?

P.title: ph-mind.c9.text
Philosophy: These old puzzles are now practical: can a language model understand, or have experiences? Philosophers disagree, and the Chinese room is quoted in AI debates every week.

P.title: ph-schools.q0.q
Philosophy: What did the Stoics say we can control?

P.title: ph-schools.q0.x
Philosophy: Focus on what's up to you.

P.title: ph-schools.q1.q
Philosophy: What did Epicurus mean by pleasure?

P.title: ph-schools.q1.o1
Philosophy: Simple pleasures and freedom from fear

P.title: ph-schools.c0.text
Philosophy: Stoics like Epictetus, Seneca and Marcus Aurelius taught that we can't control events, only our judgements and actions. Peace comes from focusing on what's up to us.

P.title: ph-schools.c1.text
Philosophy: Before worrying, sort the problem: can I control it, influence it or neither? Spend energy only on the first two.

P.title: ph-schools.c2.text
Philosophy: Stoics imagined losing what they had, not to be gloomy, but to appreciate it more and be ready for setbacks.

P.title: ph-schools.c3.text
Philosophy: Epicurus taught that a good life is a pleasant one, but meant simple pleasures: friends, conversation, bread and water, and freedom from fear and pain, not luxury.

P.title: ph-schools.c4.text
Philosophy: The Buddha taught that suffering comes from craving and attachment, and that a path of ethical living, mindfulness and wisdom can lead beyond it.

P.title: ph-schools.c5.text
Philosophy: Confucius (551–479 BCE) emphasised good relationships, respect, education and self-cultivation. His golden rule: "Do not do to others what you would not want done to you."

P.title: ph-schools.c6.text
Philosophy: Jean-Paul Sartre said "existence precedes essence": we aren't born with a fixed purpose; we create ourselves through our choices and are responsible for them.

P.title: ph-schools.c7.text
Philosophy: Albert Camus described the absurd: our search for meaning in a universe that offers none. His answer, from *The Myth of Sisyphus*: keep living fully anyway.

P.title: ph-schools.c7.viz.steps.3
Philosophy: Push again, and find joy in it

P.title: ph-schools.c8.text
Philosophy: Portuguese poet Fernando Pessoa wrote as dozens of "heteronyms", such as Alberto Caeiro, Ricardo Reis and Álvaro de Campos, each with its own life and philosophy.

P.title: ph-schools.c9.text
Philosophy: Marcus Aurelius reminded himself each morning that he'd meet difficult people today, and that he could still choose to act well. A one-minute plan for the day ahead.

P.title: ph-schools.c9.viz.items.2
Philosophy: How do I want to respond?

P.title: ph-logic.summary
Philosophy: How to reason well and spot bad arguments.

P.title: ph-logic.q0.q
Philosophy: You can't trust her argument, she's not an expert. What fallacy?

P.title: ph-logic.q0.x
Philosophy: Attacks the person, not the argument.

P.title: ph-logic.q1.q
Philosophy: Ice cream sales and drownings both rise in summer. This shows…

P.title: ph-logic.c0.text
Philosophy: An argument gives reasons (premises) for a conclusion. It's good if the premises are true and actually support the conclusion.

P.title: ph-logic.c1.text
Philosophy: An argument is valid if the conclusion must follow from the premises; sound if it's valid and the premises are true. "All cats fly; Tom is a cat; so Tom flies" is valid but not sound.

P.title: ph-logic.c2.text
Philosophy: Deduction moves from general rules to certain conclusions. Induction moves from observations to probable generalisations.

P.title: ph-logic.c3.text
Philosophy: Attacking the person instead of the argument. "You can't trust his climate data; he drives a big car" doesn't touch the data.

P.title: ph-logic.c4.text
Philosophy: Misrepresenting someone's view to make it easier to attack. "You want speed limits? So you want everyone to walk?"

P.title: ph-logic.c5.text
Philosophy: Presenting only two options when more exist. "Either you're with us or against us" ignores the many positions in between.

P.title: ph-logic.c6.text
Philosophy: Claiming one small step will inevitably lead to a disaster, without showing why. Sometimes slopes are real; the fallacy is assuming them.

P.title: ph-logic.c6.viz.steps.3
Philosophy: Disaster, with no evidence for each link

P.title: ph-logic.c7.text
Philosophy: Millions of people believe it, so it must be true. Popularity isn't evidence; many popular beliefs have turned out false.

P.title: ph-logic.c8.text
Philosophy: Ice cream sales and drownings rise together, but ice cream doesn't cause drowning: hot weather drives both. A link doesn't prove one causes the other.

P.title: ph-logic.c9.text
Philosophy: The opposite of a straw man: state your opponent's view in its strongest form before replying. If they'd say "yes, that's exactly my view", you're ready to disagree.

P.title: ph-political.q0.q
Philosophy: Who described life without government as "nasty, brutish and short"?

P.title: ph-political.q1.o1
Philosophy: Freedom can only be restricted to prevent harm to others

P.title: ph-political.q2.q
Philosophy: Who proposed separating legislative, executive and judicial powers?

P.title: ph-political.c0.text
Philosophy: Philosophers imagined life without any government to ask why we accept rulers. Their answers shaped modern democracies.

P.title: ph-political.c1.text
Philosophy: Thomas Hobbes (1651) argued that without a powerful sovereign, people would live in a war of all against all. We trade freedom for security.

P.title: ph-political.c2.text
Philosophy: John Locke argued people have natural rights to life, liberty and property, and that a government that violates them can be replaced. He influenced the American founders.

P.title: ph-political.c3.text
Philosophy: Jean-Jacques Rousseau began *The Social Contract* (1762) with "Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains". He sought a society governed by the common good.

P.title: ph-political.c4.text
Philosophy: Montesquieu argued liberty requires dividing power between legislative, executive and judicial branches, each checking the others. Portugal's constitution follows this idea.

P.title: ph-political.c5.text
Philosophy: John Stuart Mill argued the only reason to restrict someone's freedom is to prevent harm to others, not to protect them from themselves.

P.title: ph-political.c6.text
Philosophy: Broadly, liberal traditions emphasise individual rights and markets; socialist traditions emphasise equality and collective ownership. Most modern democracies mix both.

P.title: ph-political.c7.text
Philosophy: Edmund Burke valued tradition and gradual change, warning that institutions hold wisdom built over generations that radical reforms can destroy.

P.title: ph-political.c8.text
Philosophy: Plato worried that democracy lets persuasion beat wisdom. Churchill later quipped that democracy is the worst form of government, except for all the others.

P.title: ph-political.c9.text
Philosophy: After nearly 50 years of dictatorship, the Carnation Revolution of 25 April 1974 restored freedom, with a new constitution in 1976.

P.title: ph-freewill.q0.x
Philosophy: Acting on your own reasons without coercion.

P.title: ph-freewill.q1.q
Philosophy: What did Libet's experiment seem to show?

P.title: ph-freewill.q1.o1
Philosophy: Brain activity before the felt decision

P.title: ph-freewill.c0.text
Philosophy: If every event has a cause, including the firing of your neurons, are your choices truly free? Or is free will an illusion?

P.title: ph-freewill.c1.text
Philosophy: Determinism says everything that happens is fixed by prior causes and the laws of nature. Given the past, only one future is possible.

P.title: ph-freewill.c2.text
Philosophy: Some philosophers argue we have genuine freedom that isn't fully determined by prior causes. Critics ask how a choice can be both uncaused and controlled.

P.title: ph-freewill.c3.text
Philosophy: Most philosophers are compatibilists: free will means acting on your own reasons without coercion, even if those reasons have causes.

P.title: ph-freewill.c4.text
Philosophy: In the 1980s, Benjamin Libet found brain activity began before people reported deciding to move. Its meaning is fiercely debated; later work questions the interpretation.

P.title: ph-freewill.c5.text
Philosophy: Quantum physics suggests some events are truly random. But randomness doesn't seem to give us control either.

P.title: ph-freewill.c6.text
Philosophy: If free will is an illusion, can we blame or praise people? Many think responsibility still makes sense for guiding behaviour and protecting others.

P.title: ph-freewill.c7.text
Philosophy: Harry Frankfurt imagined someone who would have been forced to choose X anyway, but chose X freely on their own. Are they responsible? Most say yes.

P.title: ph-freewill.c8.text
Philosophy: Whatever the metaphysics, we experience deliberating and choosing. Some argue that experience is part of what freedom means for creatures like us.

P.title: ph-freewill.c9.text
Philosophy: Even if causes shape us, we can shape future causes: choosing environments, habits and friends that make better choices easier.

P.title: ph-meaning.q0.q
Philosophy: Who wrote "one must imagine Sisyphus happy"?

P.title: ph-meaning.q1.q
Philosophy: According to Viktor Frankl, where can meaning come from?

P.title: ph-meaning.q1.o1
Philosophy: Work, love and our attitude to suffering

P.title: ph-meaning.c0.text
Philosophy: Some traditions hold that meaning is given by God or nature; others, like existentialism, that we create our own meaning.

P.title: ph-meaning.c1.text
Philosophy: Many religions locate life's meaning in a relationship with God, following a path or escaping a cycle of rebirth.

P.title: ph-meaning.c2.text
Philosophy: For Aristotle, a meaningful life is one of flourishing: using our capacities well, in a community, guided by virtue.

P.title: ph-meaning.c3.text
Philosophy: Nihilism holds that life has no inherent meaning. Nietzsche warned of it and urged people to create new values rather than despair.

P.title: ph-meaning.c4.text
Philosophy: Camus said the honest response to a meaningless universe is revolt: to live fully, passionately and freely anyway. "One must imagine Sisyphus happy."

P.title: ph-meaning.c5.text
Philosophy: Psychiatrist Viktor Frankl, who survived Nazi concentration camps, argued meaning comes from work, love and the attitude we take to unavoidable suffering.

P.title: ph-meaning.c6.text
Philosophy: The Japanese idea of ikigai is often described as a reason for being. Western diagrams combining love, skill, need and pay are a modern addition.

P.title: ph-meaning.c6.viz.items.3
Philosophy: What you can be paid for

P.title: ph-meaning.c7.text
Philosophy: Studies suggest meaning and happiness overlap but differ: happiness is about the present and getting; meaning links past, present and future, and giving.

P.title: ph-meaning.c8.text
Philosophy: Many people find meaning not in one grand answer but in everyday things: family, friends, work done well, beauty and helping others.

P.title: ph-meaning.c9.text
Philosophy: Imagine your 80th birthday. What would you want the people closest to you to say about how you lived? That points to what matters to you.

P.title: ph-science.q0.o1
Philosophy: Prefer the simplest explanation that fits

P.title: ph-science.q1.q
Philosophy: According to Kuhn, what triggers a scientific revolution?

P.title: ph-science.q1.x
Philosophy: The old paradigm can't explain them.

P.title: ph-science.c0.text
Philosophy: Science proceeds by observation, hypothesis, prediction and testing. Results that contradict predictions force revision.

P.title: ph-science.c1.text
Philosophy: Francis Bacon (1620) urged gathering careful observations and building general laws from them, rather than reasoning from authority.

P.title: ph-science.c2.text
Philosophy: Karl Popper argued science advances by trying to refute theories. A theory that survives many attempts is corroborated, not proven.

P.title: ph-science.c3.text
Philosophy: Thomas Kuhn (1962) argued science works within paradigms. Anomalies pile up until a revolution replaces the old framework, like Copernicus over Ptolemy.

P.title: ph-science.c4.text
Philosophy: Prefer the simplest explanation that fits the evidence. Extra assumptions need extra justification.

P.title: ph-science.c5.text
Philosophy: Science uses controlled experiments to separate cause from coincidence: change one thing, keep everything else equal, and see what happens.

P.title: ph-science.c6.text
Philosophy: Before publication, other experts check a study's methods and conclusions. It catches many errors, though not all.

P.title: ph-science.c7.text
Philosophy: Astrology and homeopathy make claims that can't be tested or keep failing tests. Hallmarks include vague predictions and ignoring contrary evidence.

P.title: ph-science.c8.text
Philosophy: Scientific models simplify reality to make predictions. Statistician George Box said "all models are wrong, but some are useful".

P.title: ph-science.c9.text
Philosophy: Science's strength isn't certainty but self-correction. Theories are revised when better evidence arrives, as when continental drift was accepted in the 1960s.

P.title: ph-eastern.summary
Philosophy: Wisdom from India, China and Japan.

P.title: ph-eastern.q0.o1
Philosophy: Effortless action in harmony with nature

P.title: ph-eastern.q1.q
Philosophy: According to the Buddha, what causes suffering?

P.title: ph-eastern.c0.text
Philosophy: The *Tao Te Ching*, attributed to Laozi, teaches living in harmony with the Tao, the natural way, through simplicity, humility and effortless action (wu wei).

P.title: ph-eastern.c1.text
Philosophy: Yin and yang describe complementary opposites that depend on each other: dark and light, rest and activity. Balance between them matters.

P.title: ph-eastern.c2.text
Philosophy: Confucius stressed five key relationships, each with mutual duties, as the basis of a harmonious society.

P.title: ph-eastern.c3.text
Philosophy: Hindu traditions explore dharma (duty), karma (action and consequence), samsara (rebirth) and moksha (liberation).

P.title: ph-eastern.c4.text
Philosophy: In the Gita, the warrior Arjuna hesitates before battle. Krishna teaches him to act according to duty without attachment to results.

P.title: ph-eastern.c5.text
Philosophy: The Buddha taught that life involves suffering; suffering arises from craving; it can end; and the Eightfold Path leads there.

P.title: ph-eastern.c6.text
Philosophy: Buddhism stresses that everything changes, including the self. Clinging to what can't last causes suffering.

P.title: ph-eastern.c7.text
Philosophy: Zen Buddhism, from China to Japan, emphasises meditation and direct experience over study. Koans like "what is the sound of one hand clapping?" jolt the mind.

P.title: ph-eastern.c8.text
Philosophy: Modern mindfulness practices adapt Buddhist meditation for stress reduction. Studies show modest benefits for anxiety, stress and focus.

P.title: ph-eastern.c9.text
Philosophy: Schopenhauer drew on Indian thought; Stoicism resembles Buddhism in places. Many questions about suffering, self and virtue are shared across cultures.

P.title: ph-medieval.summary
Philosophy: Faith and reason in the Middle Ages.

P.title: ph-medieval.q0.q
Philosophy: Who wrote The Consolation of Philosophy in prison?

P.title: ph-medieval.q1.q
Philosophy: What did Aquinas believe about faith and reason?

P.title: ph-medieval.q2.q
Philosophy: When was Portugal's first university founded?

P.title: ph-medieval.q2.x
Philosophy: In Lisbon, later moved to Coimbra.

P.title: ph-medieval.c0.text
Philosophy: Augustine of Hippo (354–430) blended Christian faith with Plato's ideas. His *Confessions* is one of the first great autobiographies, exploring memory, time and the self.

P.title: ph-medieval.c1.text
Philosophy: If God is all-powerful and all-good, why does evil exist? Augustine answered that evil is an absence of good, partly caused by human free will.

P.title: ph-medieval.c2.text
Philosophy: Writing in prison awaiting execution in 524, Boethius wrote *The Consolation of Philosophy*: Lady Philosophy teaches that true happiness can't be taken away by fortune.

P.title: ph-medieval.c3.text
Philosophy: Scholars like Avicenna (Ibn Sina) and Averroes (Ibn Rushd) preserved and developed Greek philosophy. Their commentaries on Aristotle shaped European thought.

P.title: ph-medieval.c4.text
Philosophy: Avicenna imagined a man created floating in the air, blindfolded, touching nothing. He would still know he exists: self-awareness without the senses.

P.title: ph-medieval.c4.viz.steps.3
Philosophy: The self is not the body?

P.title: ph-medieval.c5.text
Philosophy: Moses Maimonides, a Jewish philosopher born in Córdoba, sought to reconcile faith with Aristotle's reason in his *Guide for the Perplexed*.

P.title: ph-medieval.c6.text
Philosophy: Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274) combined Aristotle with Christian theology, arguing faith and reason can't truly conflict because both come from God.

P.title: ph-medieval.c7.text
Philosophy: Aquinas offered five arguments for God's existence, including the "first mover": everything that moves is moved by something, so there must be a first, unmoved mover.

P.title: ph-medieval.c8.text
Philosophy: William of Ockham (c. 1287–1347) argued we shouldn't multiply entities beyond necessity. His principle became the famous "razor".

P.title: ph-medieval.c9.text
Philosophy: Medieval Europe founded universities, including Coimbra in 1290, one of the oldest in continuous operation in the world. Philosophy and theology were at their core.

P.title: ph-enlightenment.c0.text
Philosophy: Kant defined the Enlightenment in 1784 as humanity's emergence from self-imposed immaturity. His motto: *Sapere aude*, dare to think for yourself.

P.title: ph-enlightenment.c1.text
Philosophy: Baruch Spinoza, of Portuguese-Jewish descent, identified God with Nature itself, and argued for freedom of thought. He was expelled from Amsterdam's Jewish community in 1656.

P.title: ph-enlightenment.c2.text
Philosophy: Voltaire attacked intolerance and religious persecution with wit. The 1755 Lisbon earthquake inspired his *Candide*, mocking the idea that this is the "best of all possible worlds".

P.title: ph-enlightenment.c3.text
Philosophy: David Hume doubted that we can know causes, the self or miracles with certainty. Kant said Hume woke him from his "dogmatic slumber".

P.title: ph-enlightenment.c3.viz.items.1
Philosophy: The self is a bundle of perceptions

P.title: ph-enlightenment.c4.text
Philosophy: Kant argued the mind actively structures experience with space, time and causality. We know things as they appear to us, not as they are in themselves.

P.title: ph-enlightenment.c5.text
Philosophy: Diderot and d'Alembert's *Encyclopédie* (1751–1772) gathered human knowledge, including crafts and sciences, to spread reason widely.

P.title: ph-enlightenment.c6.text
Philosophy: Mary Wollstonecraft's *A Vindication of the Rights of Woman* (1792) argued women appear inferior only because they're denied education.

P.title: ph-enlightenment.c7.text
Philosophy: Adam Smith, a moral philosopher, argued in 1776 that self-interest in free markets can benefit society, like an "invisible hand". He also wrote about sympathy and ethics.

P.title: ph-enlightenment.c8.text
Philosophy: Enlightenment ideas about rights and consent of the governed fed the American Revolution (1776) and the French Revolution (1789).

P.title: ph-enlightenment.c9.text
Philosophy: In Portugal, the Marquis of Pombal rebuilt Lisbon and pushed Enlightenment-style reforms: modernising Coimbra University, secular schooling and science, though he ruled with an iron hand.

P.title: ph-modern.q0.q
Philosophy: What did Nietzsche mean by "God is dead"?

P.title: ph-modern.q0.o1
Philosophy: Belief no longer anchors Western values

P.title: ph-modern.q1.q
Philosophy: Who said it's better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied?

P.title: ph-modern.c0.text
Philosophy: Hegel saw history as ideas developing through conflict: a position meets its opposite, and a higher synthesis emerges.

P.title: ph-modern.c1.text
Philosophy: Karl Marx argued history is driven by economic conflict between classes, and that capitalism exploits workers. His ideas inspired movements and regimes with very different outcomes.

P.title: ph-modern.c2.text
Philosophy: John Stuart Mill refined utilitarianism, arguing some pleasures are higher than others: "better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied".

P.title: ph-modern.c3.text
Philosophy: Søren Kierkegaard, the "father of existentialism", stressed individual choice, commitment and the anxiety of freedom. Truth, he said, must be lived.

P.title: ph-modern.c4.text
Philosophy: Arthur Schopenhauer saw life driven by a blind, restless "will" that causes endless desire and suffering. Art, compassion and asceticism offer relief.

P.title: ph-modern.c5.text
Philosophy: Friedrich Nietzsche's famous line meant that belief in God no longer anchored Western values, and people must face creating new values.

P.title: ph-modern.c6.text
Philosophy: Nietzsche's ideal is a person who creates their own values and affirms life fully. Later misuse of his ideas by the Nazis distorted them.

P.title: ph-modern.c7.text
Philosophy: Nietzsche's thought experiment: if you had to live your life again exactly, infinitely, would you rejoice or despair? Live so you'd say yes.

P.title: ph-modern.c8.text
Philosophy: American pragmatists like William James argued an idea's truth lies in its practical consequences: what difference does it make in practice?

P.title: ph-modern.c9.text
Philosophy: Darwin's theory of evolution (1859) challenged ideas of human uniqueness and purpose in nature, reshaping philosophy, religion and ethics.

P.title: ph-thought.q0.q
Philosophy: What does Nozick's experience machine suggest?

P.title: ph-thought.q0.o1
Philosophy: We value more than pleasant experiences

P.title: ph-thought.q1.q
Philosophy: What did Galileo's thought experiment show?

P.title: ph-thought.q1.o1
Philosophy: All objects fall at the same rate

P.title: ph-thought.c0.text
Philosophy: Thought experiments test ideas by imagining scenarios we can't (or shouldn't) run for real. They reveal hidden assumptions.

P.title: ph-thought.c1.text
Philosophy: If every plank of a ship is replaced, is it the same ship? And if you rebuild the old planks into a ship, which is the original?

P.title: ph-thought.c2.text
Philosophy: How do you know you're not a brain in a vat, fed experiences by a computer? It updates Descartes' doubt for the age of simulation.

P.title: ph-thought.c3.text
Philosophy: Robert Nozick asked: would you plug into a machine giving you any pleasurable experience you want, for life? Most say no, suggesting we value more than pleasure.

P.title: ph-thought.c4.text
Philosophy: Mary knows every physical fact about colour but has lived in a black-and-white room. When she first sees red, does she learn something new?

P.title: ph-thought.c4.viz.steps.1
Philosophy: Sees red for the first time

P.title: ph-thought.c5.text
Philosophy: A teleporter scans you, destroys you and builds an exact copy on Mars. Is the copy you? What if the original isn't destroyed?

P.title: ph-thought.c6.text
Philosophy: A predictor who is almost always right offers two boxes: one with €1,000, one with €1 million or nothing. Take both, or just the second? Philosophers split.

P.title: ph-thought.c7.text
Philosophy: Rawls asked what principles you'd choose for society from behind a veil of ignorance. It's a thought experiment about fairness.

P.title: ph-thought.c8.text
Philosophy: Galileo imagined tying a heavy and light stone together: would they fall faster or slower? The contradiction showed all objects fall at the same rate.

P.title: ph-thought.c8.viz.steps.2
Philosophy: Should be both faster and slower

P.title: ph-thought.c9.text
Philosophy: Aged 16, Einstein imagined chasing a light beam. What would he see? The puzzle led him to special relativity.

P.title: ph-tech.q0.q
Philosophy: Why can AI systems be biased?

P.title: ph-tech.q0.o1
Philosophy: They learn from biased historical data

P.title: ph-tech.q0.x
Philosophy: Biased data in, biased decisions out.

P.title: ph-tech.q1.o1
Philosophy: Making AI pursue goals humans actually want

P.title: ph-tech.c0.text
Philosophy: Tools shape behaviour: cars shaped cities, phones shaped attention. Designers make value choices, whether they realise it or not.

P.title: ph-tech.c1.text
Philosophy: Who owns your data? Philosophers argue privacy protects freedom, dignity and the ability to think without being watched. The EU's GDPR gave people rights over their data.

P.title: ph-tech.c2.text
Philosophy: AI trained on biased historical data can repeat the bias: hiring tools that favoured men because past hires were mostly men.

P.title: ph-tech.c3.text
Philosophy: If a self-driving car crashes, who's to blame: the owner, the manufacturer, the programmer or the AI? Responsibility gets spread thin.

P.title: ph-tech.c4.text
Philosophy: Self-driving cars make the trolley problem real. MIT's Moral Machine survey collected millions of answers and found preferences differed across cultures.

P.title: ph-tech.c5.text
Philosophy: If machines do most jobs, how do we share the wealth, and where will people find meaning? Proposals include retraining, shorter weeks and universal basic income.

P.title: ph-tech.c6.text
Philosophy: How do we make sure powerful AI systems pursue goals humans actually want? Even well-meant instructions can be misread, like King Midas' golden touch.

P.title: ph-tech.c7.text
Philosophy: Philosophers disagree whether AI could have experiences. If it could, would it have moral status? The question shapes how we should treat future systems.

P.title: ph-tech.c8.text
Philosophy: Realistic fake images, voices and videos make it harder to trust what we see. Verification, provenance labels and media literacy become vital.

P.title: ph-tech.c9.title
Philosophy: Questions to ask of any tech

P.title: ph-tech.c9.text
Philosophy: Who benefits? Who might be harmed? What happens if everyone uses it? Can it be undone? These simple questions guide responsible use.

P.title: ph-language.summary
Philosophy: How words connect to the world.

P.title: ph-language.q0.q
Philosophy: What did the later Wittgenstein say about meaning?

P.title: ph-language.q1.q
Philosophy: I promise is an example of…

P.title: ph-language.q2.o1
Philosophy: Meaning more than you literally say

P.title: ph-language.c0.text
Philosophy: How does the word "cat" come to mean cats? Philosophers of language ask how symbols get meaning, and how we understand each other at all.

P.title: ph-language.c1.text
Philosophy: Gottlob Frege noted that "the morning star" and "the evening star" refer to the same thing, Venus, but have different senses, ways of presenting it.

P.title: ph-language.c2.text
Philosophy: In the *Tractatus* (1921), Wittgenstein argued language pictures facts, and "whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent".

P.title: ph-language.c3.text
Philosophy: Later, Wittgenstein changed his mind: the meaning of a word is its use in a "language game". "Water!" means different things to a thirsty person and a firefighter.

P.title: ph-language.c4.text
Philosophy: What do all games have in common? Nothing single, Wittgenstein said; they share overlapping similarities, like family members' faces.

P.title: ph-language.c5.text
Philosophy: J.L. Austin noticed some sentences do things: "I promise", "I resign", "I now pronounce you married" perform an action by being said.

P.title: ph-language.c6.text
Philosophy: Paul Grice noticed we mean more than we say. A reference letter saying only "he has neat handwriting" says a lot by what it leaves out.

P.title: ph-language.c7.text
Philosophy: The Sapir–Whorf idea suggests language influences how we think. Strong versions are rejected, but language can nudge attention, like Russian speakers distinguishing light and dark blue faster.

P.title: ph-language.c8.text
Philosophy: Some words seem untranslatable. Portuguese *saudade*, a longing for something absent that may never return, is often cited, though the feeling itself is universal.

P.title: ph-language.c9.text
Philosophy: Large language models produce fluent text by learning patterns in huge amounts of language. Whether they understand meaning, or just use, revives old debates.

P.title: ph-language.c9.viz.r.items.0
Philosophy: words need contact with the world

P.title: ph-beauty.q0.q
Philosophy: What was Aristotle's view of tragedy?

P.title: ph-beauty.q1.q
Philosophy: What did Duchamp exhibit as art in 1917?

P.title: ph-beauty.c0.text
Philosophy: Is beauty in the object or in the eye of the beholder? Philosophers have argued both ways for 2,500 years.

P.title: ph-beauty.c1.text
Philosophy: Plato distrusted art as a copy of a copy: a painting imitates a bed, which itself imitates the Form of Bed. He would have censored poets in his ideal city.

P.title: ph-beauty.c1.viz.steps.2
Philosophy: Painting of a bed: copy of a copy

P.title: ph-beauty.c2.text
Philosophy: Aristotle defended tragedy: watching suffering on stage arouses pity and fear and purges them, a cleansing he called catharsis.

P.title: ph-beauty.c3.text
Philosophy: Hume argued taste varies, but some judges are better: those with practice, delicacy, comparison and freedom from prejudice. Their agreement forms a standard.

P.title: ph-beauty.c4.text
Philosophy: Kant said a judgement of beauty is disinterested, not about wanting the thing, yet claims everyone should agree, unlike "I like sugar".

P.title: ph-beauty.c5.text
Philosophy: The sublime is the awe mixed with fear we feel before vast or powerful things: storms, mountains, the night sky. Burke and Kant both explored it.

P.title: ph-beauty.c6.text
Philosophy: In 1917 Marcel Duchamp exhibited a urinal signed "R. Mutt" as art. Is art defined by beauty, skill, intention or by the art world accepting it?

P.title: ph-beauty.c7.text
Philosophy: Tolstoy argued art is the transmission of feelings: the artist feels something and expresses it so others feel it too.

P.title: ph-beauty.c8.text
Philosophy: Art doesn't have to be beautiful. Goya's *Black Paintings* and war photography disturb us, yet they can be powerful and important.

P.title: ph-beauty.c9.text
Philosophy: Spend ten minutes with one painting: what do you notice first? After five minutes? Slow looking reveals far more than the average museum glance of under 30 seconds.

P.title: ph-religion.q0.o1
Philosophy: Belief is rational given the stakes

P.title: ph-religion.q1.q
Philosophy: How did Darwin challenge Paley's design argument?

P.title: ph-religion.c0.text
Philosophy: Does God exist? Can faith be rational? Why is there something rather than nothing? These questions are explored with argument, not just belief.

P.title: ph-religion.c1.text
Philosophy: Everything that begins has a cause; the universe began; so it has a cause. Critics ask why the cause must be God, and what caused God.

P.title: ph-religion.c1.viz.steps.0
Philosophy: Everything that begins has a cause

P.title: ph-religion.c2.text
Philosophy: William Paley (1802): if you found a watch on a heath, you'd infer a designer; nature is far more complex, so it needs one too. Darwin offered another explanation.

P.title: ph-religion.c3.text
Philosophy: Anselm (1078) argued God is "that than which nothing greater can be conceived", and something that exists is greater than something only imagined. Kant replied that existence isn't a property.

P.title: ph-religion.c4.text
Philosophy: Blaise Pascal argued it's rational to believe: if God exists you gain everything; if not, you lose little. Critics ask which god, and whether belief can be chosen.

P.title: ph-religion.c5.text
Philosophy: The existence of suffering is the strongest argument against an all-good, all-powerful God. Responses appeal to free will, growth or mystery.

P.title: ph-religion.c6.text
Philosophy: Some say faith goes beyond reason; others that it must be reasonable; others that it's a matter of trust, like trusting a friend.

P.title: ph-religion.c7.text
Philosophy: Atheists believe there's no God; agnostics hold we can't know. Bertrand Russell compared the burden of proof to an invisible teapot orbiting the Sun.

P.title: ph-religion.c8.text
Philosophy: Many people report direct experiences of the divine. William James studied them in 1902. Are they evidence of God, or of the human brain?

P.title: ph-religion.c9.text
Philosophy: Leibniz asked: why is there something rather than nothing? Physics, theology and philosophy offer answers, but none is universally accepted.

P.title: ph-justice.summary
Philosophy: What do we owe each other?

P.title: ph-justice.q0.q
Philosophy: What did Rawls' difference principle say?

P.title: ph-justice.q0.o1
Philosophy: Inequality only if it helps the worst off

P.title: ph-justice.q1.q
Philosophy: What's the fair way for two children to share a cake?

P.title: ph-justice.q1.x
Philosophy: It makes the cutter cut evenly.

P.title: ph-justice.c0.text
Philosophy: In Plato's *Republic*, Thrasymachus claims justice is just the interest of the stronger. Socrates spends the whole book trying to prove him wrong.

P.title: ph-justice.c0.viz.r.items.0
Philosophy: justice is harmony and good for the soul

P.title: ph-justice.c1.text
Philosophy: How should wealth and opportunities be shared? Philosophers propose equality, need, merit, free exchange or helping the worst off.

P.title: ph-justice.c2.text
Philosophy: Rawls argued inequalities are acceptable only if they benefit the least advantaged, such as higher pay for doctors that results in better healthcare for all.

P.title: ph-justice.c2.viz.steps.1
Philosophy: Does it help the worst off?

P.title: ph-justice.c3.text
Philosophy: Robert Nozick replied that if holdings were acquired fairly and transferred freely, the result is just, even if unequal. Taxation for redistribution, he argued, is like forced labour.

P.title: ph-justice.c4.text
Philosophy: After the Second World War, the UN adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948), setting rights for all people regardless of nation.

P.title: ph-justice.c5.text
Philosophy: Every right implies duties: your right to free speech implies others' duty not to silence you. Some rights demand action, like education.

P.title: ph-justice.c6.text
Philosophy: Why punish? To give people what they deserve (retribution), to prevent future crimes (deterrence), to protect society, or to reform the offender.

P.title: ph-justice.c7.text
Philosophy: Restorative justice brings offenders and victims together to repair harm, rather than just punishing. Studies show it often satisfies victims more.

P.title: ph-justice.c8.text
Philosophy: Peter Singer argued that if you'd ruin your shoes to save a child drowning in a pond, you should give to save distant children too. Distance shouldn't matter morally.

P.title: ph-justice.c9.text
Philosophy: Two children share a cake: one cuts, the other chooses. Both get a fair deal without trusting each other: a simple mechanism for justice.

P.title: ph-time.summary
Philosophy: What is real, what is now?

P.title: ph-time.q0.q
Philosophy: What gives time its direction in physics?

P.title: ph-time.q1.q
Philosophy: Who said you can't step in the same river twice?

P.title: ph-time.c0.text
Philosophy: Augustine wrote: "What then is time? If no one asks me, I know; if I wish to explain it to one who asks, I know not." It's still puzzling.

P.title: ph-time.c1.text
Philosophy: Presentists say only the present exists. Eternalists say past, present and future are equally real, like places on a map; relativity seems to support them.

P.title: ph-time.c2.text
Philosophy: Physics laws mostly work the same backwards, yet we remember the past, not the future, and eggs break but don't unbreak. Entropy gives time its direction.

P.title: ph-time.c3.text
Philosophy: Zeno argued a flying arrow is motionless at every instant, so motion is impossible. Calculus later explained how motion emerges from instants.

P.title: ph-time.c4.text
Philosophy: You can't step in the same river twice, said Heraclitus: the water has flowed on, and you've changed too. Reality is change.

P.title: ph-time.c5.text
Philosophy: Parmenides argued the opposite: change is an illusion, and true reality is one, unchanging and eternal.

P.title: ph-time.c6.text
Philosophy: Physics has no special "now", yet we experience one. Is the flow of time a feature of the world or of our minds?

P.title: ph-time.c7.text
Philosophy: Philosophers use "possible worlds" to think about what could have been: in some possible world, you became an astronaut.

P.title: ph-time.c8.text
Philosophy: Epicurus argued death is nothing to fear: "Where death is, I am not; where I am, death is not." Others find the loss of future goods a real harm.

P.title: ph-time.c9.text
Philosophy: Seneca wrote that life is long if you know how to use it. Most of us waste time, not lack it.

P.title: ph-time.c9.viz.items.0.r
Philosophy: Life is long if well used
